messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 44
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tattoo Artist
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something, Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell

Vignette:
Malee Srisawat is a 44-year-old Thai-American woman who has worked as a tattoo artist for nearly fifteen years, building a loyal clientele at a small studio in a mid-sized Pacific Northwest city. She came to the intake appointment accompanied by her husband, though she asked him to wait in the lobby — a detail that, in itself, spoke to something she was still working out about needing help at all.

Approximately eighteen months ago, Malee was working a closing shift at the studio when a neighbouring dry-cleaning business experienced a catastrophic solvent leak. A cloud of perchloroethylene seeped through the shared ventilation system before anyone understood what was happening. Malee noticed the smell first — something sharp and synthetic beneath the familiar scent of ink and latex — and then the burning in her throat, the sudden heaviness in her chest, the way the room seemed to tilt. By the time emergency services arrived, she was on the floor of her own studio, unable to move her legs reliably, unable to call out. Paramedics in full protective gear came through the door, and in the minutes that followed, Malee was strapped to a gurney, her arms secured, an oxygen mask pressed onto her face by hands she could not see clearly. She described this period — perhaps twenty minutes in total — as the most terrifying of her life. She could not remove the mask. She could not sit up. She could not ask them to stop or slow down or explain what was happening to her body. She simply had to endure.

She was hospitalised for four days. The physical recovery was, by medical accounts, complete. What did not resolve was the way those twenty minutes had lodged themselves somewhere that medicine could not reach.

In the months that followed, Malee found herself alert to things she had never consciously registered before. The antiseptic smell of a hospital corridor — encountered during a routine follow-up appointment, then again when her husband had minor surgery — produced an immediate and overwhelming physical response: her heart hammering, her hands going cold, the sensation of the gurney straps returning across her forearms. She began declining to accompany family members to medical appointments, offering practical excuses that satisfied everyone except herself. What she had come to believe was that the smell itself was a kind of warning, that her body was telling her something real was about to happen again.

At the tattoo studio, the difficulties were more complicated and harder to conceal. Tattooing requires a client to observe the artist's hands closely and continuously, and Malee had always welcomed that intimacy. Now she found that the sustained sensation of being watched — a client's eyes tracking her movements, a colleague glancing over her shoulder to admire her line work — produced a creeping, almost unbearable self-consciousness that she could not reason her way out of. She had begun positioning herself so that her back was more often to the wall, rearranging her station in ways that her colleagues noticed and quietly questioned.

More disruptive still was what happened when clients, as they inevitably did, asked her to adjust her grip, reposition their arm, or hold a particular angle for longer than felt comfortable to her. These were ordinary professional negotiations. But any moment in which she felt compelled to comply — her hands guided by someone else's instruction, her body positioned according to another person's need — could bring on a sudden, vertiginous sense of wrongness that she struggled to name and could not always contain. She had cancelled three bookings in the past two months, citing illness. Her income had begun to reflect the absences.

Her husband noticed the cancellations before she told him about any of it. It was his quiet, persistent concern — and, she admitted, a fear that she was losing something she had spent fifteen years building — that finally brought her to the clinic. What frightened her most, she said at the end of the intake, was not the memories themselves but the possibility that she would never again feel at ease inside her own studio, inside the work that had always felt most fully like hers.
